issues: Wrong legal basis in the summary. The summary says the Commission decided 'under Article 25(2) of Directive 95/46/EC'. The decision was adopted 'having regard to ... Directive 95/46/EC ... and in particular Article 25(6) thereof'. Article 25(6) is the provision that empowers the Commission to find a third country adequate. Article 1(1) of the decision refers to Article 25(2) only for the purposes of the adequacy test.

Source note error. The note says the self-certification list is in Recital 8. It is in Recital (7) ('...maintain and make available to the public a list of organisations self-certifying their adherence to the Principles...'). Recital (8) is about suspending data flows.

Location note is misleading for 2000. The Commission did not sit in the Berlaymont in 2000: the commissioners moved to the Breydel building at the end of 1991, and the Berlaymont was handed back only from 1 July 2004 (Wikipedia, Berlaymont building). The coordinates are in the right quarter, a few hundred metres off, so only the note needs rewording.

Everything else checks out on the Publications Office text of OJ L 215, 25.8.2000: the date, 'Done at Brussels, 26 July 2000', the Article 1 quote, the Principles and FAQs issued by the US Department of Commerce on 21 July 2000, self-certification, and the public list (FAQ 6: 'The Department (or its designee) will maintain a list of all organizations that file such letters'). The UK National Archives facsimile PDF (legislation.gov.uk/eudn/2000/520/pdfs/eudn_20000520_adopted_en.pdf) also has the Article 1 quote and the signing line.

The cited Wayback URL could not be re-opened: web.archive.org resets connections from this sandbox. That source is set to PENDING, and the official Publications Office (CELLAR) copy is added as a CONFIRMED source.

fieldFixes.summary: On 26 July 2000 the European Commission, acting under Article 25(6) of Directive 95/46/EC, decided that the 'Safe Harbor Privacy Principles' and frequently asked questions issued by the US Department of Commerce on 21 July 2000 ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data sent to US organisations that signed up to them. Companies joined by self-certifying their adherence, with the Commerce Department keeping a public list.
fieldFixes.locationNote: 'Done at Brussels'. In 2000 the Commission sat in the Breydel building while the Berlaymont was being renovated (1991-2004). The coordinates mark the Berlaymont/Schuman quarter and are approximate.

issues: Overstated 'only' in the significance. It calls IE6 'The only mass deployment of P3P'. Internet Explorer was the only mainstream browser to act on P3P, but it was not the only deployment: Mozilla shipped some P3P features for a few years before removing the code by 2007 (Wikipedia, P3P). 'By far the largest' is accurate.

The significance also says sites 'learned they had only to send the right tokens, true or not'. No cited source documents sites actually doing this. The IEInternals footnote supports the underlying point: 'There's no technical means by which the browser can enforce the claims in the P3P statement'. The corrected wording rests on that footnote.

Both quotes were re-fetched and are verbatim (FOUND). The press release is dated 'REDMOND, Wash., March 21, 2001' and says IE6 will ship 'as part of the Windows XP operating system later this year'. It confirms the deny/downgrade/accept logic and the Medium (default) rule: 'If a third party has no compact policy, third-party cookies will be rejected.' The IEInternals page's ms.date is 2010-06-05, and it carries the 2/20/2012 update. IE6 was released in August 2001 (Wikipedia gives August 24, 2001), which fits 'shipped later in 2001'.

fieldFixes.significance: By far the largest deployment of P3P (Internet Explorer was the only mainstream browser to act on it) turned a site-authored policy into a gate key. As Microsoft itself noted, the browser had no technical means to check what a site's tokens claimed, so the right tokens got cookies through whether or not they were true.

issues: The summary narrows section 215. It says the FBI could seek orders 'in international-terrorism investigations'. As enacted, new FISA section 501(a)(1) covered 'an investigation to protect against international terrorism or clandestine intelligence activities'. The quote on the record already includes that wording; the summary drops the second limb.

Where it happened: the Act was enacted when President Bush signed it in the East Room of the White House on 26 October 2001 (White House release, 'Remarks by the President at Signing of the Patriot Act, Anti-Terrorism Legislation'). The Capitol is an acceptable seat for an Act of Congress, but the location note should say where it was signed.

Everything else was re-fetched from GovInfo and checks out. The quote is verbatim, with a fresh cache. The margin note '<<NOTE: Oct. 26, 2001 - [H.R. 3162]>>' is present. Section 216's amendment of 18 U.S.C. 3127(3) inserts 'dialing, routing, addressing, or signaling information transmitted by an instrument or facility from which a wire or electronic communication is transmitted'. '26 October 2001, six weeks after 11 September' is 45 days, so six weeks is fair.

fieldFixes.summary: Enacted on 26 October 2001, six weeks after the September 11 attacks, the USA PATRIOT Act (Public Law 107-56) let the FBI apply for court orders requiring the production of 'any tangible things (including books, records, papers, documents, and other items)' for an investigation to protect against international terrorism or clandestine intelligence activities (section 215). It also extended pen-register and trap-and-trace orders to the 'dialing, routing, addressing, or signaling information' of wire and electronic communications (section 216).
fieldFixes.locationNote: The legislature's seat. President Bush signed the Act into law in the East Room of the White House.

fieldFixes.summary: On 6 November 2007 Facebook announced that 44 websites, including Fandango and Travelocity, were using Beacon to send users' actions on their sites, such as purchases, to Facebook for display to friends. eBay said it would add Beacon for its sellers' listings in early 2008. Beacon was initially opt-out: if a user forgot to decline, the action was shared. After weeks of protest Facebook switched it to opt-in, and on 5 December 2007 Mark Zuckerberg apologised ('We simply did a bad job with this release, and I apologize for it') and added a control to turn Beacon off completely.
